video_title: BlackRock's Tony Kim on AI's Next Winners? Chips, Memory, Robotics & Quantum
gist: Tony Kim, head of BlackRock's global technology team, argues AI has triggered a full data-center rebuild that has shifted roughly $30 trillion-plus of global tech market cap into chips/hardware (versus ~$10 trillion in legacy software/internet and ~$22-23 trillion in the 'Mag 7'), explains how he allocates about 90% of capital to a 3-year compute/memory 'now' window while reserving the rest for 2030-dated frontier bets like quantum, orbital data centers, and robotics, and predicts China will dominate humanoid-robot manufacturing while the West leads on AI 'brains.'

themes.theme: The AI-driven market-cap and data-center rebuild

insights.claim: Tony Kim estimates global tech market cap now splits roughly into $10 trillion-plus in legacy software/services/internet, $22-23 trillion in his redefined 'Mag 7' category (which now includes Microsoft as compute-centric rather than pure software), and $30 trillion-plus in chips and hardware — a mix he says was roughly reversed before the AI era, with the shift systematically occurring over the last four years.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Quantifies a historic reallocation of tech market cap toward the physical compute layer, a structural argument for staying overweight chips/hardware versus legacy SaaS/internet names.
insights.quote: There's roughly 10 plus trillion market cap in software and services and internet... There's 22 23 trillion in Mac 7 and then there's another 30 plus trillion in chips and hardware.

insights.claim: Kim says the base layer of AI compute has risen roughly 10,000x in cost/value terms since the 'AI era' began around 2023 — a server that cost $10,000 in the cloud-computing era is now effectively a million-dollar server.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A striking single-number illustration of how much more capital-intensive AI infrastructure is versus the prior cloud-computing paradigm, useful for framing capex growth expectations.
insights.quote: So the base layer of compute went up 10,000x. $10,000 server is a million dollar server.

insights.claim: Kim frames the pre-AI cloud computing era (roughly 2000-2020) as a business built on a thin, commoditized compute layer (CPUs plus hard drives, sold cheaply) with nearly all the margin captured by SaaS built on top; AI has now inverted this, moving the majority of value and margin into the compute layer itself.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism behind the 'SaaS apocalypse' sell-off — margin structure across the entire tech stack is being reorganized around compute/token creation rather than application-layer software.
insights.quote: you're reselling, you're building this massive application on a very very thin layer of compute... AI happens... everything changed.

insights.claim: Kim says roughly $1 trillion of AI capex this year and about $10 trillion over the next five years is fundamentally being spent to move data shorter physical distances — from kilometers between buildings down to meters, centimeters, and now millimeters within a chip — because shrinking that distance is what increases bandwidth while driving up power and heat requirements logarithmically.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Reframes the entire AI infrastructure buildout as a physics-constrained problem (power density, heat, bandwidth) rather than a simple compute-quantity story, which should guide where investors expect the next bottlenecks and winners to emerge (packaging, cooling, optics, power).
insights.quote: the trillion dollars of capex this year and the 10 trillion over the next five years that are coming is to move data centimeters and millimeters. That's AI.

insights.claim: Kim expects the data center to shift from a copper-based to a light-based (optical) architecture as a primary way to manage the power density, heat, and bandwidth constraints created by AI compute, alongside new power architectures (800-volt systems, eventually solid-state transformers) to reduce energy losses at each voltage step-down.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Identifies optical interconnects and next-gen power electronics (800V systems, solid-state transformers) as specific sub-sectors of the data-center buildout likely to see outsized capital allocation.
insights.quote: we're going from a regime of copper to a regime of light.

themes.theme: The "RAM apocalypse" and the rising primacy of memory

insights.claim: Kim argues that while AI infrastructure discussion has focused on compute, memory intensity is now increasing even faster (the 'RAM apocalypse'), because next-generation AI systems are increasingly designed to emulate the human brain, which is more memory-intensive than compute-intensive, requiring more high-bandwidth memory, stacked DRAM, and flash tightly integrated with chip architecture.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Suggests memory/storage suppliers may be structurally underappreciated relative to compute/GPU names as the next leg of the AI infrastructure trade, since agentic AI systems require persistent memory of context and behavior.
insights.quote: the human brain is very memory intensive and today [AI] is more compute intensive. But as you see it with RAM apocalypse, the memory intensity is just skyrocketed.

insights.claim: Kim highlights a structural duration mismatch driving the memory shortage: building a new memory fab takes three to four years, but demand is surging today, meaning the market cannot simply spend its way out of the current shortage in the near term.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Explains why memory pricing power and shortages could persist for years even as capital floods in, since fab lead times structurally cap near-term supply response.
insights.quote: it takes three or four years to build a chip fab for a memory fab but yet everyone there's a shortage today... there's this like mismatch of demand supply duration.

insights.claim: There are only a handful of major global memory producers, and Kim notes the market is grappling with how to underwrite the demand premium for a name like SK Hynix given how supply-constrained the sector is and how long that scarcity might persist.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock / host
insights.so_what: Flags valuation uncertainty in memory stocks as a live debate — the scarcity premium is real but its durability is the key open question for investors.

insights.claim: Kim relays an anecdote from a major memory company that it cannot find enough engineers to design custom memory for AI chip co-design, and is having to repurpose software programmers into memory co-design architects — evidence of a severe talent bottleneck in a highly specialized, historically neglected discipline.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A human-capital constraint (not just capital or fab capacity) that could further extend memory scarcity and pricing power beyond what capex alone would suggest.
insights.quote: we cannot get people to design custom memory... we got to repurpose some of these software programmers into memory codesign architects.

themes.theme: Capital allocation framework: the 3-year "now" vs. the 2030 frontier

insights.claim: Kim allocates roughly 90% of his investment activity to a three-year time horizon he calls 'the now' — arbitrating which companies are winning, losing, or stagnating within the current AI/compute/memory buildout — while reserving a smaller share of time and capital for longer-dated, 5-10 year 'frontier of the frontier' bets.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A concrete, reusable time-horizon-based capital allocation rule investors can apply when deciding how much of a portfolio to commit to proven near-term AI infrastructure winners versus speculative long-dated technology.
insights.quote: within this three-year window... 90ish% something like that... is going in.

insights.claim: Kim says he made AI-adjacent investments before 2019-2021 — prior to the LLM/generative AI wave — based purely on the intuition that AI compute demand of some form would be needed, illustrating that his longest-duration bets are made on structural direction rather than a specific technology's exact form.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A model for pre-hype-cycle investing: back the directional thesis (compute demand rising) years before the specific winning technology (LLMs) becomes obvious.
insights.quote: My intuition was that we will need AI compute of some form... I didn't know that this LLM... would happen but you're thinking about future architectures.

insights.claim: Kim observes that a remarkable number of frontier technologies converge on a 2030 target date: utility-scale, error-corrected million-qubit quantum computers; SMR/fusion nuclear power with regulatory approval; classical-computing-defined AGI timelines; 800-volt power architectures; solid-state transformers; and orbital data centers at meaningful scale.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Identifies 2030 as a clustering catalyst year across multiple unrelated deep-tech sectors, useful for investors building out longer-dated venture or thematic portfolios timed to converge around that window.
insights.quote: All roads converge to 2030.

insights.claim: Kim's screen for long-duration bets is explicitly non-incremental: he seeks nonlinear, asymmetric potential rather than what's simply fashionable today, warning that a company riding today's trend without a believable 5-year-plus future will suffer exit-multiple compression as growth decelerates.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A valuation-discipline warning: momentum-driven AI investments without a durable multi-year growth story risk becoming 'yesterday's news' and getting re-rated down even if the underlying trend was real.
insights.quote: you become yesterday's news in five years even though you are cool today... that really has a huge impact on your exit multiple.

insights.claim: Kim expects the next 12 months to bring recurring scare narratives (roughly every six months) — a 'chip apocalypse,' war shocks, high interest rates, insufficient capex financing — but believes the underlying compute/memory/data-center buildout will keep plowing through each scare rather than being derailed by it.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A base-case forecast that periodic AI-infrastructure sell-offs on scare headlines should be treated as noise rather than trend breaks, useful for timing entries during drawdowns.
insights.quote: it seems like every six months there's a scare... X apocalypse... but I think through it all... this compute wall, the memory wall... will just plow through.

insights.claim: Kim says he is hopeful/expects major foundation-model labs to go public within the next 12 months and believes there will be substantial market appetite for those IPOs.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A specific, time-bound catalyst (foundation-lab IPOs within 12 months) for public-market investors to watch for new AI investment vehicles.
insights.quote: I'm hopeful excited to see the big labs go public in the next 12 months.

themes.theme: Robotics: China's manufacturing lead vs. the West's "brain" lead

insights.claim: Kim counts roughly 130-140 robotics companies in China today and expects 30-40 potential Chinese robotics IPOs this year alone, versus zero to two in the United States in the same period, attributing the gap partly to China's shallower private markets pushing companies to use public markets as a funding mechanism earlier than in the US.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A stark, quantified signal that Chinese public markets could become the primary listing venue for humanoid/industrial robotics investment exposure well ahead of the US.
insights.quote: there's 130 140 robotics companies in China... I see 30 40 potential IPOs this year in China alone this year and there's what zero one two in the United States.

insights.claim: Kim models a humanoid robot as requiring two distinct 'brains' — a baseline LLM for language/communication and a separate world-model brain for motor function and physical perception — with the physical body/embodiment (especially hands and limbs) being the hardest and most manufacturing-intensive part to build.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A useful decomposition for evaluating robotics investments separately along 'brain' (software/AI labs) versus 'body' (manufacturing/hardware) value chains.
insights.quote: you have a a brain that will be built... a world model to perceive the world and motion... and an embodiment of intelligence... the body arms limbs hands are probably the hardest thing.

insights.claim: Kim believes China may lag the West in robotic 'brain'/world-model development but leads decisively in the physical manufacturing of robot bodies (via its broader Japan/Korea/China Asian manufacturing complex and EV-platform manufacturing scale), and predicts a likely future of hybrid products pairing Chinese-manufactured robot bodies with Western AI brains.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should expect cross-border supply chains in robotics (Western AI IP + Asian manufacturing) rather than fully vertically-integrated national champions, similar to today's semiconductor/EV supply chains.
insights.quote: you might have is ultimately you can mix and match Chinese physical robot with a western brain and I know that's happening.

insights.claim: Kim's personal area of highest interest in robotics is not industrial/manufacturing robots but social/companionship robots addressing loneliness and eldercare, citing that some of the best-performing companies globally today are nursing-home operators, and that aging populations across Asia (birth rates below 1.0 versus a 2.1-2.2 replacement rate) create a large addressable market for companion robots.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Identifies a non-obvious, demographically-driven robotics use case (elderly companionship, not warehouse automation) that could be a large but under-covered market opportunity.
insights.quote: some of the best performing companies in in the world are nursing home companies... I think robots... if you could embody some intelligence, empathy... could unlock a really really interesting market.

themes.theme: Semiconductors: the mispriced "commodity" with the highest margins

insights.claim: Kim argues chip companies have long been mischaracterized as commodity businesses when in fact they carry the highest profit margins of any sector in the world — higher than software, pharmaceuticals, industrials, or telecom — a mispricing he attributes to venture capital historically refusing to fund semiconductor startups.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Challenges the conventional 'chips are commoditized' narrative, arguing the sector's real economics (duopoly pricing power from decades of consolidation) justify premium valuations rather than commodity-like multiples.
insights.quote: they have the highest profitability of any company in the world of the sector is chip companies. They're higher margins than software, pharmaceuticals, industrials, telecom, anything.

insights.claim: Kim notes the chip industry consolidated over roughly 20 years from hundreds of competing companies down to just a few survivors in each category, creating duopoly-like pricing power — the structural opposite of a commodity market.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Explains the durability of current chip-company margins as a function of decades of consolidation and lack of new entrants (due to VC underfunding), suggesting the moat is structural rather than cyclical.
insights.quote: there were hundreds of chip companies and then systematically over 20 years now there's just a few... those that have survived are behemoths with huge pricing power.

themes.theme: The enterprise "token flow" and PE roll-ups rebuilding old industries

insights.claim: Kim frames the future enterprise as a 'token flow': intelligence (tokens) comes in from foundation models, interacts with a proprietary data/context layer (what Palantir calls an 'ontology'), and agents built on top of that context layer are what create defensible value — companies must position themselves somewhere in this token flow (creating, reselling, or repackaging tokens) or risk irrelevance.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A mental model for evaluating any enterprise-software investment post-AI: does the company sit inside the token flow with proprietary context, or is it a commoditized wrapper at risk of disintermediation?
insights.quote: follow the flow of tokens... If you're not in that flow, it's a problem.

insights.claim: Kim sees rising demand for full-stack AI 'inference clouds' / edge-AI providers that package tokens with developer tooling for smaller and medium businesses, effectively inserting themselves into the token flow as a last-mile layer rather than remaining pure infrastructure or pure application vendors.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Identifies inference/edge-cloud providers as a structurally advantaged category versus pure application-layer software companies that lack their own token supply.

insights.claim: Kim describes an emerging business model where companies abstract away an entire back-office function (e.g., "I will do all of your insurance claims processing") and charge a flat fee dramatically below the prior cost of that function, rather than selling discrete software tools — collapsing the question of whether a company is an app, service, or compute provider.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: Signals a shift from software-as-a-tool to software-as-a-full-service-replacement pricing model, which could compress incumbent services revenue (BPO, claims processing, insurance administration) sharply.
insights.quote: Today you used to pay a hundred, I'll charge you 20.

insights.claim: Kim points to private equity and venture firms buying legacy, low-AI-adoption companies specifically to rebuild their operations on an AI-native stack, citing General Catalyst's Creation Fund and its portfolio company Long Lake acquiring AMEX Global's travel business as an example of a smaller AI-native company acquiring a much larger legacy incumbent.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock / host
insights.so_what: A concrete, named example of the 'buy-and-rebuild-with-AI' roll-up strategy in action, worth tracking as a template that could repeat across other legacy service industries.

insights.claim: Kim describes a rubric where a lean, AI-native company of roughly 500 people can generate the revenue of a traditional 10,000-person organization, arguing the central question for legacy incumbents is whether they can adapt fast enough before AI-native competitors or PE-backed roll-ups displace them.
insights.speaker: Tony Kim, BlackRock
insights.so_what: A headcount-productivity heuristic (20x revenue-per-employee) for identifying which traditional industries are most vulnerable to AI-native disruption or roll-up strategies.
insights.quote: a new company with 500 people that can do and generate the revenue of 10,000 people.
